h1: State labelling rules for spirits in India
title: Spirits Labelling Rules in India | Craft Beer School
desc: A process-level guide to what a spirits label in India must carry, why each state adds its own rules and how approvals work.
teaser: One whisky can need a different label in every state it is sold in. Here is why that happens and what goes on each one.
standfirst: A whisky label in India answers to several rulebooks at once: national food and metrology rules plus each state's excise department. This guide explains the layers at process level so marketing, legal and supply chain teams know why labels take so long.
sections: Three layers of rules sit on one label

The first layer is national food law. FSSAI standards for alcoholic beverages cover what a product called whisky must be and what the label must declare, including statutory health warnings such as the line that consumption of alcohol is injurious to health and a warning against drinking and driving.

The second layer is legal metrology, which covers packaged goods in general. It asks for the name and address of the manufacturer or packer, net quantity in millilitres, MRP inclusive of all taxes, the month and year of manufacture or packing and a consumer care contact.

The third layer is the state. Because alcohol is a state subject, each state excise department can add its own requirements and must usually approve the label before the product is sold there. That third layer is where most of the variation lives.

State requirements change, so treat this as a list of the kinds of things states ask for rather than a checklist:

  • A line restricting sale to that state, such as "for sale in" followed by the state name.
  • An excise adhesive label, hologram or security sticker applied to each bottle.
  • A barcode or QR code linked to the state's track and trace system.
  • The state's approved MRP for that pack.
  • Registration or approval references issued by the excise department.

Some states supply the security labels themselves and charge for them. Others require the brand to print codes in a set format. Always work from the current state notification or a licensing consultant, not from last year's artwork.

In many states a brand registers its labels and prices for the excise year, often aligned to April to March. Registration typically needs label artwork, product details, lab analysis and fees, though the documents vary. A new SKU, a new pack size or a new design usually needs a fresh approval.

That turns label changes into calendar planning. A brand that wants a new festive pack in November may need artwork approved in summer. A design tweak as small as moving the age statement can trigger resubmission in every state. Our guide to how MRP changes work covers the price side of the same process.
Words on a whisky label carry legal weight

Some label terms have defined meanings. An age statement on a blend refers to the youngest whisky in it. Calling a product Scotch means it was distilled and matured in Scotland for at least three years in oak. Single malt means malted barley distilled at one distillery, usually in pot stills. In India, products sold as whisky are often blends of neutral spirit with malt spirit. The FSSAI standards describe what may be called whisky and malt whisky.

Marketing teams sometimes want words like "aged", "reserve" or "small batch" for tone. Some are defined, some are not and some can mislead if the liquid does not match. Legal and quality teams should check every descriptive word against the current standards before artwork goes to a state.
Advertising rules reach the label too

Direct advertising of alcohol is restricted in India. That pushes brands to rely on the pack itself, which makes the label one of the few places a brand can speak. It also means the label is scrutinised. Claims about health, strength as a selling point or appeal to young people are off limits in practice and in principle.

Brand extensions such as soda or water under a whisky name raise questions of surrogate advertising. Our guide to surrogate advertising rules covers that ground. For labels, the rule of thumb is to describe the product accurately and let the design do the rest.
Why one blend becomes many SKUs

Put the layers together and the arithmetic is simple. One blend sold in 750 ml, 375 ml and 180 ml across twelve states can need 36 approved labels, each with its own MRP, codes and state text. A gift pack doubles some of those. Every approval has its own renewal date.

For supply chain, that means labels cannot be swapped between states. A label printed for one state is waste in another. For data teams, it means the label version is part of the SKU. For marketing, it means a redesign is a programme of work, not a single file sent to the printer.
What your team gains from knowing the rules

Teams who understand the layers stop treating label delays as someone else's failure. Marketing plans artwork around approval windows. Supply chain orders state labels on time. Legal reviews claims early instead of at the last minute. This is process knowledge, not legal advice.

A practical first step: take one label from each of your two largest states and mark every element by the layer that requires it: national food law, metrology or state excise. The state-only elements are the ones to track on your approval calendar.
faqs: Does every state need a separate whisky label?
Often yes. Many states require their own text, MRP, security labels or codes, so one product usually needs a label version per state.
What must a spirits label in India show?
Typically the product name, manufacturer details, net quantity, MRP, date of manufacture or packing, statutory health warnings and state-specific items. Check the current rules for each state.
